newsitem.title: SRI LANKA: Drought, terrorism hit Sri Lanka economy in 1996.
newsitem.headline: Drought, terrorism hit Sri Lanka economy in 1996.

text.p: Sri Lanka's economic growth slowed in 1996, tripped up by the nation's civil war and a drought which caused agricultural output to fall, the Central Bank said in its 1996 annual report released on Wednesday.
It said the country's gross domestic product (GDP) grew by a provisional 3.8 percent in 1996, compared to 5.5 percent in 1995.
"A prolonged drought depressed agriculture production by 4.6 percent," the report said. Agricultural output grew by 3.3 percent in 1995.
Inflation was sharply higher at 15.9 percent in 1996, largely reflecting the drought-induced food shortages and world market prices, the Central Bank said.
The drought also affected electricity supply, which is largely generated by water power, hitting industrial production in the first half of the year.
"The problem was compounded by a few incidents of urban terrorism, which appear to have affected business confidence," the report said.
Tamil Tiger separatists carried out a suicide attack on the Central Bank and bombed a packed commuter train in 1996.
The Liberation Tigers of Tamil Eelam are fighting for a separate homeland for minority ethnic Tamils in the island's north and east.
The 13-year war also raised Sri Lanka's defence expenditures to 44.12 billion rupees ($747.8 million) in 1996 against 43 billion in the previous year.
"An early settlement to the problem in the north and east would be a plus factor in this regard," the report said.
The security fears led to a sharp fall of 25 percent in tourist arrivals, one of the main foreign exchange earners for Sri Lanka.
Sri Lanka's manufacturing sector, however, showed remarkable resilience despite the drought and power cuts, growing 7.3 percent, from 10.2 percent in 1995, the report said.
After slowing in the first half of the year, exports and imports picked up during the second half mainly due to an improvement in tea prices, the report said.

The drought in 1996 mainly affected non-plantation agriculture and coconut production. Tea production, after record output in 1995, rose a further five percent while tea prices increased by 44 percent to reach record levels, the report said.
The Central Bank also said exports grew 13 percent in 1996, while imports increased by seven, resulting in a reduction in the trade deficit to 9.4 percent of GDP.

Despite all the negative factors plus "an escalation in the cost of subsidies and a shortfall in privatisation proceeds, the overall budget deficit was contained at 7.8 percent of GDP," the report said.
The budget deficit was 8.3 percent in 1995.
The Central Bank said in the report that large budget deficits have been the main factor destabilising the macro-economic situation in Sri Lanka.
A heavy fiscal burden has emerged as a result of the rapidly rising costs of a high volume of public debt and public sector salaries in addition to the rising defence expenditure, the report said.
Interest on public debt, public sector salaries and wages, and pensions take up nearly 70 percent of total government revenue, leaving only 30 percent to meet other expenditures, it said.
The Central Bank said the deficit could be narrowed only by eliminating structural weaknesses in the budget and reducing public sector inefficiencies through civil service reforms.
($1=59 rupees)
